question: Three fatty acids esterified to one glycerol leave no polar group at all, so a _____ will not dissolve in water and collects instead as a droplet.
questions: Adrenaline does not reach the fat itself but unlocks it, phosphorylating the protein that coats the droplet so the lipases can begin cutting a _____ apart.
Because it cannot dissolve in blood, a _____ travels in a lipoprotein particle, and the level of those particles is what a routine blood test reports.
abstract:
A triglyceride, or triacylglycerol, is three fatty acids joined to a single glycerol molecule, and it is the form in which fatty acids are stored. With all three of the glycerol's hydroxyls taken up in ester bonds the molecule keeps no polar group, so it is insoluble in water and gathers as fat droplets in the cytoplasm. That is what makes it worth using as a fuel store, since fats yield more than twice as much energy per unit weight as carbohydrates and let an animal carry a given reserve in less than half the body weight. Building one ends with diacylglycerol acyltransferase, which esterifies the third fatty acid onto a diacylglycerol and catalyses the committed, rate-limiting step of the pathway. Plants run the same chemistry into their seeds, which is where seed oil comes from; oats hold more of it than any other cereal.

Getting the energy back out is lipolysis, and three enzymes take the fatty acids off in turn: adipose triglyceride lipase, hormone-sensitive lipase and monoacylglycerol lipase, leaving free fatty acids and glycerol. The store is locked rather than merely kept, because perilipin-1 coats the droplet and holds the first lipase's coactivator away from it until adrenaline, acting through protein kinase A, phosphorylates the perilipin and lets go. That is not the only switch, and work on adipose tissue in the bone marrow, which resists the usual cues, describes a route driven by low glucose and low insulin that needs no adrenaline at all. Because a triglyceride will not dissolve in blood either, it travels inside lipoprotein particles, chylomicrons from the gut after a fatty meal and very-low-density lipoprotein from the liver, whose cargo lipoprotein lipase cuts up at the tissue that needs it. Those particles and the remnants they leave are what a blood triglyceride reading measures, and their disordered handling raises the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
